title: Leasing the jazz masters, rack jobs and bootleg discovery
summary: Jazz sales collapsed in the rock-and-roll era, so the masters were leased; Harry Fox then revealed a licensee had retitled songs to avoid royalties.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay. What happened? You had some trouble with those Lp's down the line. What happened with those recordings?
Well we leased them out to a company. They was supposed to do -- We only leased them out for -- say for a certain area, rack job. They wanted to do a --
Why were they leased out?
Well they were covering a different area that we were covering. It wasn't supposed to be in the same area -- We wasn't in that market. They was gonna do.a -- that time, you had a -- what we call

"rack jobs." You know, they was gonna cover like apartment stores.

The revenue was good that was coming from the albums, you know. But we found out -- like when you lease records out, like a lot of records -- like big companies, they'll lease a master out to another company, you know -- for a budget line, you know.

Well this particular time that -- I can tell you the reason why we did lease them out, because that was a time -- around that time, the 50's and the 60's, when the rock and roll, rhythm and blues had came in so big that it actually just had killed the sale of jazz.
We couldn't even -- The only thing that we were doing with an album like Edmund Hall was with colleges, Overseas -- we shipped it overseas. We got a -- through Rank Records.
We released it over there in Japan through RCA -- distributed it for us.
And we were doing good overseas with it,

but we wasn't doing anything here in the states. It was selling, but, you know, jazz had dropped down like, you know.
Because the whole market -- everybody was going for the -- stream-of (inaudible) over to Alan Freed -- they were taking over the rhythm and blues.
The small bands was as its height that time. And that was just an era that jazz almost dropped off the market in this country, you know.
If you wasn't over -- go overseas, -- you wasn't making a living. So most of the guys cut out and went to Europe, you know.
A lot of the top jazz musicians went to Europe and stayed, going back and forth.
But it was a market for it, but not a big market. So we had an offer from a company that showed what they --

They called them something else. And they -- no, this is so and so song.
And I come up and I found that Edmund Hall's album they had released, and they had took one of the pop songs and called it something else, you know. To keep from paying royalty on it.
And that's when they stopped -- they stepped in and we stopped --
That was the beginning of the -- finding out about these bootleg things. And we started tracking down on all these budget lines, you know.
If you had something that wasn't moving on your label, you lease it out to a budget line, like Pickwit.
Pickwit was a big budget line -- Pickwit Records was a big budget line that did albums -- that leased albums from Columbia, Decca, and everybody else.
